doc.title: Pierre Boussaguet interviewed by Matthieu Jaffre, Aix en Provence, France, July 28, 2020

title: From accordion to bass
summary: His accordion teacher's advice and the 'sweetest lie' led him to electric bass; he reflects on the bassist's role and Ron Carter.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up a first guitar or banjo, self-taught

blocks.x: Can you describe for us how you came to the bass, and how was your first gig as a jazz player?

So the first question is how I moved from accordion to the bass. My teacher on accordion, you know especially for dancing music you play only the right hand because you have a rhythm section so you don’t need to play the chords and the bass on the left. And that was much more interesting unconsciously with the harmonies on any waltz or any dancing song, I would stop my teacher and say, “Yeah but you know this is not good, you put a C on the bass then we move to F and you should put a C5 augmented to move there because of the melody.” And one day he told me, he said, “I don’t get it. You’re supposed to play the right hand and your brain, your spirit, your focus is on harmony, about the bass note. He said, “Well if you want to play some kind of modern instrument, you should just move to electric bass,” and he told me what I called the sweetest lie I heard in my life. He told me, he said, “I guarantee if you practice half an hour for two months, the bass, it’s nothing.
Yes, but after two months I realized that it was not that easy.

So basically, to answer your question, I was, for some reason, I was interested a lot in the fundamentals of music and the harmony, which is actually I discovered later on, that’s the job of a bassist. It’s not just to play a groove. To me that’s totally wrong. It’s to create a fundamental voice that is a voice by itself but always nourishing what the orchestra says, help the soloist of trying — exactly like Ron Carter put it just in a few words, I’m talking too much, Ron Carter said, “Our job is to find the good notes.” That’s perfect. So from then on I switched to bass and the Hot Club at that time. That was my first jazz concert in the theater. I didn’t want to go because at that time because at that time I didn’t know jazz.
